chunks: Al-Hasan ibn Sam'a, from more than one, from Aban, from Abd al-Rahman ibn Abi Abdillah, from Humran, who said:

I asked him about al-sukna and al-'umra, so he said: 'The people are subject to their conditions; if his condition was for his life, it remains for his life, and if it was for his descendants, then it is for his descendants as he stipulated, until they perish, then it returns to the owner of the house.'

key_terms.اَلسُّكْنَى: Sukna: a type of usufruct contract where a person grants another the right to live in a property for a specified period or life.
key_terms.اَلْعَقِبُ: Descendants/Offspring: referring to the progeny or heirs of the grantor, who may inherit the usufruct rights.
key_terms.اَلْعُمْرَى: 'Umra: a type of usufruct contract where a person grants another the right to use a property for their lifetime, often with reversion to the grantor or their heirs.
key_terms.حَيَاتَهُ: His life: referring to the duration of the grantor's life, indicating the contract's term.
key_terms.شُرُوطِهِمْ: Their conditions: the specific terms and stipulations agreed upon by the parties in the contract.
key_terms.صَاحِبُ الدَّارِ: Owner of the house: the original owner of the property who retains ownership rights after the usufruct period ends.

ai.seo_question: What is the legal difference between sukna and 'umra contracts regarding their duration and reversion of property?
ai.summary: This hadith from Shaykh al-Tusi’s *Tahdhib al-Ahkam* clarifies the duration of *sukna* (residence) and *'umra* (lifetime usufruct) contracts, emphasizing that the rights are strictly bound by the stipulations (*shurut*) agreed upon by the parties. It establishes a hierarchical succession where the grantor’s life takes precedence, followed by his descendants until their line ends, at which point the property reverts to the original owner, reflecting the Shia juristic principle of honoring contractual intent in temporary property rights.
